children: OTTAWA--Canada's financial-industry watchdog plans to soften capital requirements for smaller lenders in a bid to boost competition and break the hold of handful of major banks on the industry.

The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions said Thursday it is proposing a "made-in-Canada" approach, dubbed the competitive prudential initiative, that seeks to increase the capacity of the financial system to take reasonable risks, compete and innovate while still maintaining resilience.

The regulator said it would lower capital intensity for lending by small- and medium-sized banks--including federal credit unions--in residential mortgages, small- and medium-sized-business lending and corporate lending.

"This is our most ambitious effort to date to level the playing field in Canadian banking without materially impacting the resilience of the system," Peter Routledge, superintendent of financial institutions, said.

Routledge said his office thought the initiative is making consequential changes to competitive capacity by giving smaller deposit-takers greater room for prudent risk-taking. "This is a significant step forward, but not the end of our ambitions," he said.
Ottawa, in its latest annual budget, handed OSFI a secondary responsibility focusing on fostering financial-services competition in the country, opening a door for the planned changes.

The budget plan introduced by Prime Minister Mark Carney's government in November unveiled changes to the regulator's remit to add a component that would ensure competition considerations such as market effects and the burdens of compliance are more clearly and consistently reflected in regulatory oversight.

The regulator, which is an independent government agency responsible for prudential regulation and the supervision of the country's banks, proposes what it said would be targeted changes to the capital-adequacy guidelines for small- and medium-sized banks that will allow for an increased capacity for risk and improve the competitive balance in capitalization between them and the country's six biggest banks.

This will include adjustments to align capital requirements for specific classes of underlying risks, and simplifying the capital structure for these smaller banks and credit unions. It also includes lower capital requirements for government-sponsored venture capital fund investments.

In addition, OSFI is revising covered bond limits to give both smaller and major banks additional access to stable funding but still ensuring they continue to hold enough unencumbered assets to support depositors and other creditors in stress or resolution.

The revisions would introduce different covered bond limits for domestic systemically important banks and smaller lenders to reflect differences in their balance sheets and bond-funding capacity. The current limit caps assets pledged for covered bonds at 5.5% of an institution's total on-balance-sheet assets. This would rise to 7% for the biggest banks and set a limit of 15% of domestic on-balance-sheet assets for smaller banks.

The budget introduced in November also included plans to encourage entry into the mid-sized-banking market by exempting foreign-bank subsidiaries with less than 8 billion Canadian dollars, the equivalent of about US$5.6 billion, in equity from present rules requiring that a certain level of their voting shares be publicly traded.

The regulator said institutions would still be expected to hold capital in proportion to their risks. Instead, the proposed changes address areas where existing requirements may mean disproportionate constraints on smaller institutions relative to both the underlying prudential risk and to competitive industry dynamics.

The regulators plans will be open for public consultation until Feb. 17. Final changes are set to come into effect at the start of November 2027 or Jan. 1, 2028, depending on whether an institution's fiscal year ends on Oct. 31 or Dec. 31.
